name: Yohimbine
short: Small studies in people on opioid treatment: yohimbine by vein (8 on methadone) set off withdrawal and craving; by mouth (10 on buprenorphine) withdrawal, higher blood pressure, more opioid-seeking.
text: In a meta-analysis of seven randomized placebo-controlled trials of yohimbine on its own in men with erectile dysfunction, serious adverse reactions were infrequent and reversible; the abstract does not list them. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 86 men with erectile dysfunction without clearly detectable organic or psychological causes, yohimbine hydrochloride was taken by mouth for eight weeks (the abstract does not give the number in each group); only 7% of patients rated tolerability fair or poor, most adverse experiences were mild and there was no serious adverse event. A 2001 review states that, in acute and long-term studies, yohimbine has been found relatively free of side effects over a dose range for which the abstract gives no figures, and that at much higher doses the most frequent effects are raised blood pressure, a slight anxiety-provoking action and more frequent urination, all easily reversible when yohimbine is stopped. A 1992 case-report letter is titled 'Overdose of yohimbine' (title only; no abstract). Interactions with opioid treatment: in a double-blind, placebo-controlled study whose title names yohimbine-induced withdrawal and anxiety symptoms, yohimbine given into a vein to 8 patients on methadone set off objective and subjective opioid withdrawal and raised craving for opioids; the results were compared with those from a pool of 9 healthy volunteers, and the authors conclude that methadone-maintained patients are sensitive to medicines that facilitate noradrenaline, experiencing greater physiologic and psychological symptoms, including an increase in craving, and that medicines that increase noradrenaline should be used with care in opioid-dependent people. In a double-blind, randomized crossover study in 10 heroin-dependent people stabilized on buprenorphine, yohimbine by mouth increased opioid-seeking (in a laboratory task in which the volunteers could work to earn units of the opioid hydromorphone or money, yohimbine significantly increased a measure of their demand for hydromorphone, demand inelasticity, compared with placebo) and produced dose-dependent rises in blood pressure (about 15 mmHg systolic and 10 mmHg diastolic, described as clinically modest) and in opioid withdrawal symptoms; the authors report that these effects occurred without clinically significant subjective distress or elevated craving, whereas the methadone study reported raised craving.
